paper_title: Factorized MLLM Embeddings for Composed Image Retrieval

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve a target image given a reference image and a modification text. Although recent approaches leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown significant progress, we argue that the MLLM's compositional understanding remains underutilized. This stems from directly mapping composed queries into a retrieval embedding via contrastive supervision alone, without explicitly resolving the intended visual modifications. In this work, we introduce Factorized MLLM Embeddings (FactEmbed), which decouples compositional query comprehension from building discriminative embeddings. Rather than directly projecting the composed query into a single embedding without internal reasoning, FactEmbed employs a set of factorized latents that simulate the intended visual modifications via an intermediate target imagination objective. This process encourages the latents to ground into target semantics before forming discriminative representations for retrieval. Subsequently, to propagate these factorized representations throughout the model for retrieval, we optimize a factor-level contrastive loss while distilling the decomposed representations into a deeper attention layer of the MLLM. Finally, for efficient inference, we retain the [EOS] token to establish a global-level embedding on top of these factorized latents, while we exploit the mean-pooled factorized latents to rerank a short candidate list at negligible cost, as both are produced by the same forward pass. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks.

Extensive evaluations demonstrate that FactEmbed outperforms prior works across CIR benchmarks. 1. Introduction Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) aims to retrieve target image from gallery using composed query, consisting of reference image and modification text [1]. CIR allows users to express their search intent through relative descriptions: they may provide an image and specify how the desired result should differ from it. This paradigm is appealing when users can recognize desired image by its visual relation to Corresponding author. reference, but cannot easily describe the target itself. Recently, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as powerful foundation for CIR, owing to their ability to deeply fuse visual and linguistic information within unified autoregressive representation space [2, 3]. common strategy is to finetune an MLLM contrastively by compressing the multimodal query and the target image into single embedding, typically obtained from the final [EOS] token, and directly optimizing their similarity [2, 4 6]. Despite its effectiveness, this formulation exposes key limitation: forcing direct mapping onto single embedding provides no explicit signal for the MLLM to exploit its compositional understanding capability to resolve the requested edit before forming discriminative embedding. To overcome this, we aim to decouple query comprehension from discriminative embedding learning, allowing the model to first simulate the requested edit, i.e., imagine the target, and then build its retrieval embedding upon the imagined target. We present FactEmbed, which realizes this intermediate step through compact set of factorized latents that parse the query before producing the final embedding. These factorized latents are prepended to the [EOS] token in the input sequence, serving as information bottlenecks that decompose fused multimodal queries into factor-level components. This explicit decomposition enables FactEmbed to isolate specific visual attributes and distinguish the factors the text modifies from those it preserves, in contrast to direct contrastive mapping which only implicitly infers the modified embedding. To encourage each latent to capture different details in the target image, we adopt target imagination objective parameterized by lightweight decoder over these latents. Given coarse layout prior of the target, the latents are trained to imagine the residual fine-grained factors that the prior cannot explain. Constraining reconstruction through these bottlenecks forces the latents to cluster semantically coherent target factors to maximize the coverage. This provides structural supervision without requiring explicit reasoning traces or dense annotations, thereby allowing the model to implicitly simulate the specified edit. Reconstruction alone, however, shapes the latents generatively without ensuring their utility for retrieval: paired query 1 and target could be faithfully decomposed yet embedded in incompatible coordinate spaces. We address this by adapting target imagination for retrieval in two ways. First, we apply factor-level InfoNCE objective directly on the factorized latents, ensuring that the decomposed factors are aligned for retrieval rather than only for reconstruction. Second, we distill the decoders factorized representation into the attention maps of the latents at deeper layer, transferring the fine-grained decomposition from the auxiliary head into the backbone layers accessed during retrieval. Lastly, we assign complementary roles to the two outputs produced in single forward pass. Positioned prior to the [EOS], the factorized latents allow [EOS] to integrate the decomposed factors into global retrieval embedding, while [EOS] is optimized as single retrieval embedding for efficient retrieval. Yet, as fine-grained information is inevitably diluted when aggregating multiple factors into single discriminative embedding, we rerank short candidate list retrieved by [EOS] using the mean-pooled latents. This complementary structure allows FactEmbed to achieve fast global recall via single [EOS] token while precision is significantly boosted by recovering fine-grained factor evidence during reranking. Because both representations originate from single forward pass and the mean-pooled latent adds only one vector per image, this design complements the global embedding with factor-level evidence without additional encoding or heavy storage overhead. Combined with our MLLM data augmentation, FactEmbed achieves state-of-the-art results on CIR benchmarks, outperforming both CIR methods and general-purpose embedding models. 2. Related Work Composed Image Retrieval. CIR aims to retrieve target image from gallery given reference image with modification text that states how the desired result should differ from it [1, 79]. Earlier works [1, 1014] attempted to resolve representational conflict by performing the composition inside CLIP [15] or BLIP [16, 17] embeddings. Then, since collecting high-precision annotations for CIR incurs significant cost [18, 19], two parallel lines of research have been actively explored: learning with noisy CIR annotations [20] and zero-shot approaches [21]. While the former stream attempted to mitigate the impact of noisy annotations by leveraging loss dynamics [22], similarity curves [23], MLLM-constructed anchor set [24], or unlearning process [25], zero-shot approaches aim to bypass the high cost of collecting annotated triplets [2631]. Notably, recent zero-shot methods also anticipate the target, either by generating proxy image [30] or by leveraging world model [31]; in contrast, our imagination is embedded within the embedding model itself, requiring neither generative model nor an additional inference pass. More recently, LLMs and MLLMs have been widely adopted in CIR owing to their strong comprehension capabilities. CIR-LVLM [4] adapted local MLLM for CIR by introducing intent-aware instructions with learnable soft prompts, while ReCALL [2] proposed MLLM-based triplet augmentation strategy by diagnosing the blind spots of adapted MLLM retriever. To further exploit the comprehension capability of LLMs, CCIN [32] and FIRE-CIR [33] incorporated an external LLM at query time to decompose the query at the attribute level, which, however, incurs substantial inference overhead, with FIRE-CIR further requiring verification linear in the number of candidates. Thus, in this work, we adapt local MLLM to exploit its inherent comprehension capability; whereas prior MLLM-based methods [2, 4] directly map the composed query onto single embedding, we encourage the model to decompose the query within single forward pass and build the retrieval embedding on top of the decomposed factors. Multimodal Retrieval with MLLMs. MLLM embeddings are being extensively studied in multimodal retrieval where complex comprehension is required [3436]. VLM2Vec [37] initially used the last hidden state of the [EOS] token of causal MLLM. Yet, as [EOS] is not designed to generate embeddings, different methods are being studied, e.g., meanpooling [3840] and multi-vector embeddings [4143]. Also, integrating computation via explicit reasoning [44], latent rollouts [45], or reinforcement-learned generative embeddings [46] is another prominent line of research. Our work resembles the stream of appending small bank of learned tokens whose hidden states become the representation [47, 48]. None of these works, however, constrains what an individual token should represent. In contrast, we leverage target reconstruction as structural supervisory signal, forcing each factorized latent to ground and specialize in spatially coherent regions of the target scene. Compact Latent Representations. Representing an input as small set of latents has been studied extensively across fields. Retrievers used it for late interaction [4952], Perceiver [53, 54] exploited latents to decouple compute from input size, DETR [55] used them as object queries to perform object detection, and slot attention [5658] utilized slots to decompose the scene into object-wise regions by normalizing the attention across latents. FactEmbed adopts the same competitive normalization in its decoder to induce factor-level specialization, but keeps the MLLMs forward pass intact, thereby preserving kernel optimizations such as FlashAttention [59]. 3. FactEmbed: Factorized MLLM Embeddings Task. Given query = (Ir, ) consisting of reference image Ir and modification text , the goal of Composed Image Retrieval (CIR) is to retrieve the target image = It that depicts the reference after the described modification. Overview. As shown in Fig. 1, FactEmbed adapts an MLLM to produce CIR embeddings, utilizing shared backbone to encode both the multimodal query and the target image. Rather than mapping the input directly to single vector, we first introduce learnable factorized latents into the multimodal input, on top of which the [EOS] embedding is formed. This provides the model with the capacity to represent the complex query as structured set of compositional components. To ground these latents in the visual content of the target image, we train them to reconstruct the targets patch features beyond coarse layout prior, process we refer to as target imagination. We perform this reconstruction by attaching lightweight decoder at an intermediate layer of the MLLM, which allows the deeper layers to transform the decomposed factors into discriminative representations for retrieval. For retrieval training, we apply InfoNCE [60] at two levels: factor-level loss encourages the factorized latents to contribute to retrieval by matching the query and target latents via optimal transport, while an instance-level loss optimizes the global embedding. In this way, the imagined decomposition propagates fine-grained evidence into compact embedding that remains efficient for retrieval. 3.1. Factorized Latents with Target Imagination Motivation. CIR requires modifying specific visual concepts given text instructions (e.g., replacing an item). However, directly mapping composed query to global embedding in an MLLM provides no explicit mechanism for disentangling the visual attributes to be modified from those that should remain invariant. To overcome this, we introduce compact set of factorized latents whose explicit job is to parse the scene into structured factors. By decomposing the representation, these latents are designed to give the model room to express the instructed modification on the relevant factors without distorting the others. 1 Factorized Latents. Determining the MLLM layer ℓ for target imagination governs trade-off; when the decoder is attached too early, the factorized latents may lack sufficient contextual fusion of multimodal inputs to imagine the target, while attaching it too late leaves insufficient subsequent layers to transform the decomposed factors into discriminative retrieval embedding. Also, OT matching consistently outperforms MS matching strategy on both benchmarks, supporting our choice of OT for factor-level matching. What Does the Decoder Imagine? We further apply FactEmbed to stronger MLLM backbones in Tab. 6. Specifically, we observe that upgrading the backbone from Qwen2.5-VL-7B to Qwen3-VL-8B improves R@1 by 2.65 points on the CIRR test set, exceeding the 1.60 points gain reported by ReCALL [2] for the same backbone transition. This demonstrates that FactEmbed scales more effectively with improved backbone capabilities. The performance gains further extend to Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B, backbone already specialized for retrieval, where FactEmbed achieves top performance across most metrics. 5. Conclusion In this work, we present FactEmbed, framework that better exploits the MLLMs compositional understanding capability to simulate visual edits by decoupling compositional query comprehension from learning discriminative embedding. To structure query comprehension, we prepend factorized latents that act as an information bottleneck, trained to imagine the residual target factors beyond coarse layout prior that groups semantically coherent visual factors of the target without dense annotations. We then bridge generative imagination and discriminative retrieval by optimizing factor-level InfoNCE loss via optimal transport and distilling the decoders alpha masks into the MLLMs deeper attention maps. At inference, the [EOS] token serves as globallevel embedding to perform initial retrieval, while the meanpooled factorized latents, produced in the same forward pass, rerank short candidate list at negligible cost. Extensive evaluations show that FactEmbed achieves state-of-the-art performance, suggesting that factor-level supervision on top of instance-level matching improves MLLM-based CIR. Limitations. Despite its effectiveness, FactEmbed has several limitations. First, using fixed ignores the input complexity since no explicit supervision specifies the number of semantic factors. Exploring query-adaptive latents and matching schemes across varying set sizes remains for future work. Second, while full-factor retrieval achieves higher accuracy, we mean-pool the latents for efficient reranking, unexploiting part of the fine-grained information. Incorporating Matryoshka representation learning [79] into factor representations may preserve accuracy of full-factor matching near single-vector storage costs. Lastly, our evaluation is limited to CIRR and FashionIQ; thus, generalizability as unified multimodal retriever requires further verification. 8 A. Additional Visualizations for Imagination In this section, we present additional results for target imagination in Fig. 5. Following the protocol in Sec. 4.4, we jointly apply PCA to the ground-truth DINOv2 [61] feature maps and our imagined representations for visualization. Although the shared color mapping between both visualized images is partly facilitated by the target layout prior, we remark that this prior provides only highly coarse, average-pooled 2 2 spatial layout. Consequently, the reconstruction of details (e.g., geometry and position) demonstrates that our factorized latents successfully capture rich spatial positioning and object geometry, allowing the decoder to synthesize the spatial maps across local regions. B. Diversity of Factorized Latents To analyze whether each factorized latent specializes in distinct concepts, we examine the cosine similarity between factorized latents both within the same instance and across different instances (Tab. 7). Specifically, we compare our approach against two baseline variants: one where learnable latents are prepended to the [EOS] token without additional constraints, and another where the factor-level InfoNCE objective is introduced. As discussed in Sec. 3.3, applying the factor-level InfoNCE alone without the imagination objective Limag (b) increases the similarity among latents within each instance, causing them to collapse into single instance-level representation. This is because the retrieval objective only requires the latents to be collectively discriminative across instances, providing no incentive for individual latents to take on distinct roles. Furthermore, this representation collapse becomes even more pronounced when the per-latent mean vector (computed across the dataset) is subtracted from each latent, indicating that the latents share instance-specific rather than factor-specific information. In contrast, incorporating our imagination and distillation objectives (c) yields the lowest within-instance similarity, with clear margin after removing the per-latent mean (0.548 vs. 0.599 and 0.841). This indicates that our framework encourages the latents to take on distinct roles, whereas naıvely employing multi-vector latents with retrieval objective drives them toward shared representation. Note that the latents without any auxiliary objective (a) also exhibit low within-instance similarity. We attribute this phenomenon to the fact that the latents are orthogonally initialized and largely retain this initial bias due to the lack of direct supervision. Indeed, these latents do not benefit retrieval: even with efficient reranking, they achieve an average of 73.21 on Refined-CIRR and 79.60 on the CIRR test set, falling below the baseline without latents (74.65 and 79.80), where the averages follow Tab. 1 and Tab. 2, i.e., (R@1 + Rsubset@1)/2 and (R@5 + Rsubset@1)/2, respectively. In contrast, under the same setting without post-training, our latents raise these scores to 76.05 and 82.35 (Tab. 5 (f)), confirming that they are not only distinct but also informative for retrieval. C. Inference Cost natural concern with multi-vector representations is that they trade retrieval quality for memory footprint and query latency [42, 47]. To address this, Tab. 8 quantifies the inference overhead on the CIRR validation set (2,297 gallery images) using single NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell GPU. Crucially, the forward pass of the query encoder dominates the end-to-end latency pipeline, requiring 353ms per query at batch size 1 and an average of 164ms per query at batch size 32. In contrast, scoring the gallery using only the [EOS] embedding requires only 0.06ms per query. Our efficient reranking procedure, which re-scores the top-100 shortlist with the sum of the cosine similarities from each [EOS] and mean factorized vector, adds one extra vector per image to the index and 0.17ms per query at batch size 1 (0.003ms amortized), which only induces less than 0.05% overhead on the total latency. We adopt this design as our default inference configuration, as its storage footprint remains comparable to, or slightly smaller than that of recent CIR methods that maintain multi-vector galleries [10, 14, 22, 23, 25, 32]. When storage and compute budgets permit, however, the full latent variant can be preferred, as full OT matching offers slightly higher R@1 (Tab. 4). Note that its time overhead remains marginal at the scale of the CIRR validation gallery, but both its storage (K vectors per image) and its scoring cost grow linearly with the gallery size, whereas efficient reranking only rescores fixed top-100 shortlist. D. Additional Implementation Details In this section, we elaborate additional implementation details. While we use base learning rates of 2 105 and 4 105 to train DoRA modules attached to the pretrained backbone parameters for CIRR and Fashion-IQ, respectively, we apply 4104 as the learning rate to modules such as the factorized latent and imagination decoder since our newly introduced components are trained from scratch. For the training schedule, we use 3,000, 500, and 350 steps across the three stages for CIRR, and 3,000, 350, and 350 steps for FashionIQ. While Stage 1 could technically be trained jointly with the later stages, the competing dynamics between Limag and LNCE slow down the formation of factorized latents, requiring substantially longer training to converge. Isolating Stage 1 to train only the decoder and the latents with Limag removes this competition and further allows bypassing the upper layers of the MLLM backbone, yielding substantially more compute-efficient setup: Stage 1 completes in approximately 13 hours on 4 RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell 9 Figure 5. In other words, instructions are often rarely exhaustive; they specify what should change while leaving everything else implicit. Consequently, single composed query can often be satisfied by multiple candidate images in the gallery. To address this, prior works have leveraged LLM/MLLMs to sharpen the query itself to disambiguate the instruction [32, 33], enlarged the clean paired triplets [2, 18, 19, 35]. Similarly, we follow ReCALL [2] to augment training triplets by pairing each reference image with its mined hard negative instances, and Table 8. Operating on FactEmbed after Stage 2, our augmentation pipeline consists of two phases: hard negative mining and contrastive captioning. During the mining phase, we follow ReCALL to extract hard negative instances Ih for each reference image Ir that ranks above the ground truth It, which are then passed to the contrastive captioning phase. F.1. Contrastive Captioning (a) Impact of Stage3 Post-training on CIRR dataset. Following ReCALL [2], we convert each mined hard negative Ih into new positive triplet (Ir, , Ih), where an MLLM writes minimal modification text that transforms Ir into Ih. In practice, however, we found this pipeline to be both noisy and costly. Since mined hard negatives frequently serve as valid targets for (Ir, ) themselves and the captioner observes only Ir and Ih, we observed that the captioner has no cue to separate Ih from It. As result, it often returned unchanged, producing duplicate queries with conflicting positives (9% and 11% of the samples that survived ReCALLs VQA filter on CIRR and FashionIQ). This pipeline was also inefficient: the local MLLM captioner frequently violated the required output format, with 37% (CIRR) and 56% (FashionIQ) of instances failing on the first pass and 9% and 12% remaining unresolved even after six retry rounds, and the subsequent VQA filter added another full inference pass. We thus streamline the pipeline with two modifications, while keeping the remaining instructions of ReCALLs captioning prompt unchanged. First, we employ contrastive captioning strategy, which additionally presents the original target It alongside Ir and Ih, and instruct the model to describe Ih such that the text no longer applies to It. Note that It serves purely as conditioning signal and is omitted from the augmented triplet. Second, we replace the local captioner with GPT-5.6-luna [80] via the batch API, which can follow both the contrast instruction and the output format in single pass, removing the retry loop and separate verification stage. Compared with the ReCALLs two-image prompting strategy on 100 sampled mined queries per dataset, we found that our contrastive captioning successfully yields an edited mod- (b) Impact of Stage3 Post-training on FashionIQ Dataset. Numbers above the bars denote the absolute gains over stage 2 baseline. ification text while the two-image prompting strategy produced 27.0% (CIRR) and 33.0% (FashionIQ) of modification texts unchanged. Furthermore, among the edited queries, we found that 30.1% (CIRR) and 10.5% (FashionIQ) of the modification texts rewritten by the two-image prompting strategy were judged by GPT-5.6-luna to describe the original target It better than the mined target Ih, while our contrastive captioning reduced this reversal rate to 7.0% and 0.0%, respectively. Consequently, as shown in Fig. 6, our contrastive captioning yields larger gains than the augmentation strategy of ReCALL on most metrics, with comparable results on Rs@1 of Refined-CIRR. This demonstrates that our streamlined pipeline is not only more efficient, as it requires neither caption retry loop nor separate verification stage, but 11 also yields higher-quality augmentation. We remark that other than these modifications, we followed ReCALL [2] to mine five hard negatives per composed query, resulting in 57,476 (CIRR) and 56,499 (FashionIQ) captioning requests. This incurs one-time cost of only $22.82 (CIRR) and $26.17 (FashionIQ), which is highly economical compared to renting GPU servers to deploy local MLLM, which often struggles with strict output formatting and thus requires repeated retries. F.2. Hard Negative Filtering Hard negative mining occasionally yields near-duplicate instances that are virtually identical to the annotated target despite holding distinct identifiers in the same dataset. Rewriting such pair forces the model to generate text that separates two near-identical images, teaching the retriever to incorrectly push them apart. To prevent this, we filter out these pairs prior to contrastive captioning based on visual feature similarity via DINOv2 [61] before we query the MLLM to write the captions. Specifically, we encoded each image using frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 backbone and mean-pooled the patch tokens into single descriptor, discarding hard negative candidates (Ih) that exhibit cosine similarity exceeding 0.99 with the original target (It). This filtering step removes 743 CIRR instances and 277 FashionIQ instances out of 58, 219 and 56, 776 mined pairs, respectively. For Stage 3, we additionally filter mislabeled original triplets: when mining with the Stage 2 model, we also record the rank of the ground-truth target, and drop the 3% of original triplets whose ground truth is ranked lowest. F.3. Post-training Finally, for the post-training stage, we optimize our model using the total objective, described in Eq. 8, similarly to stage 2. Note that we construct each batch for CIRR by grouping an original triplet with its MLLM-augmented counterparts following [2]. This strategy supplies high-quality in-batch hard negatives, explicitly encouraging the model to discern subtle visual differences. F.4. Limitation of Contrastive Captioning While our contrastive captioning mitigates noisy supervision in both the original and augmented triplets, limitation remains when scaling up the augmentation. Contrastive captioning conditions each rewrite only on the original target It, so it reduces ambiguity between It and hard negative but not among the multiple hard negatives mined for the same composed query. As more hard negatives are mined per query, i.e., each pair of reference image Ir and modification text , we expect these sibling hard negatives to increasingly overlap in semantics, so that modification text written for one may equally describe another, introducing false negatives within the augmented set. An effective aug12 mentation strategy for CIR therefore requires conditioning across both the original and augmented sets, so that each generated instruction captures features that distinguish its target from all other candidates of the same query. Nevertheless, since the augmented triplets consistently improve CIR performance in our experiments, we will publicly release them to facilitate future research. G. Qualitative Results In Fig. 7, Fig. 8, Fig. 9, and Fig. 10, we present qualitative comparisons between FactEmbed and our baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct [67] fine-tuned via DoRA [63]). In CIR, modifying reference image with text often projects the query into broad semantic space where multiple target images can be considered valid matches. Therefore, rather than restricting our analysis to Top-1 prediction, we examine the Top-8 retrieved results to better assess the overall alignment between the composed query and the retrieved distribution. In the first example of Fig. 7, which belongs to the dress category of FashionIQ dataset, the query specifies an item that is more fashionable and party wear and is cream and brown with animal print. While both models successfully capture the desired color scheme, FactEmbed ranks candidates that accurately reflect the fine-grained animal print pattern higher than the baseline. In the second example, the baseline struggles with structural modifications, incorrectly retrieving an item with short sleeves at Rank-2 and entirely ignoring the requested strap detail at Rank-3. Conversely, FactEmbed strictly adheres to these fine-grained structural constraints across the top ranked candidates. Fig. 8 further highlights common failure mode in standard contrastive learning, which fails to handle negative constraints. For the query containing the phrase instead of superman logo, the baseline fails to disentangle the negated element, retrieving images containing the superman logo. In contrast, FactEmbed successfully suppresses the negated visual element while maintaining the core semantics of the reference image. This gap in multimodal understanding extends to the opendomain CIRR dataset. As shown in the first example of Fig. 10, the query requires the model to identify map displayed on the screen of smartphone. While the baseline is easily distracted by generic smartphone images, FactEmbed accurately grounds the text modification into the precise visual context. Also, for queries involving relative counting or relational reasoning (e.g., second example), the baseline exhibits severe lack of compositional understanding. Overall, we find that the baseline trained with standard contrastive learning often ignores the comparative conditions, while FactEmbed captures these relationships more faithfully. Figure 7.
